 Claimed at 62 and Regret It? At 67 You Can Switch the Checks Off and Earn 8% a Year Until 70. Nothing Has to Be Paid Back, and Your Spouse’s Benefit on Your Record Stops Too
 By Vilma Rios 
 Published November 20, 2026, 5:13am ET · 4 min read 
 Tax Master desk. Editor: Vilma Rios .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 At full retirement age, early claimers can suspend checks and earn 8% a year until 70, with no repayment of benefits already received.
 Pausing a $1,400 check until 70 lifts it to about $1,736 a month, with break-even around age 82.
 Suspension also halts spousal benefits on your record, except for a divorced spouse, so households should add up the lost checks first.

 Consider a retiree, a 67-year-old who took Social Security at 62 mostly because the checks were available. Five years on, his savings have held up, he still works part time, and the reduced check feels like a mistake he can’t undo.
 He can undo a large part of it. At full retirement age, he can tell Social Security to stop the checks and earn 8% [ 1 ] a year in delayed retirement credits until 70. Nothing gets paid back. The fine print: anyone collecting a spousal benefit on his record loses that check for the same months.
 Social Security Has a Pause Button at Full Retirement Age
 The rule is called voluntary suspension , and the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 set its current form. Once you reach full retirement age, which is 67 [ 2 ] for anyone born in 1960 and later, you can ask the Social Security Administration (SSA) to suspend payments. You can ask orally or in writing. [ 3 ] The suspension starts the month after your request, and payments restart automatically the month you reach age 70 [ 3 ] .
 For anyone born in 1943 or later [ 1 ] , credits build at 2/3 of 1% a month. Withdrawing your application works differently. Form SSA-521 lets you cancel up to 12 months after approval, but you have to repay every dollar you and your family received, including Medicare premiums and taxes that were withheld. Suspension carries no repayment. The five years of checks he already received are his to keep.
 Run the Math: a $1,400 Check Grows to $1,736
 Assume his full-retirement-age benefit is $2,000 a month. Taking it at 62 cut it by 30% [ 2 ] , to $1,400. If he suspends for the 36 months from 67 to 70, the credits add 24% to the reduced check. That brings him to $1,736 a month before cost-of-living increases. He never gets back to $2,000, but he closes most of the gap.
 The pause costs him $50,400 in checks he doesn’t receive. In return, he collects $336 more every month for the rest of his life. He breaks even about 150 months after 70, at roughly age 82½. Each future COLA, like the 2.8% increase for 2026, is applied to the larger base. If he’s the higher earner, the bigger check is also the one his widow could step up to.
 Your Spouse’s Benefit on Your Record Stops Too
 The 2015 law ended the old “file and suspend” strategy. Under SSA rules, anyone receiving benefits on your record can’t collect them while your benefit is suspended. A divorced spouse is the exception and keeps receiving benefits. [ 3 ] Any benefit you collect on someone else’s record is suspended as well.
 His wife’s own retirement benefit, if she has one, keeps paying. Any spousal top-up on his record stops for the same months, and spousal benefits earn no delayed credits for the wait. Add her lost checks to his before deciding.
 Paused Checks Open a Roth Conversion Window
 Under 26 U.S.C. § 86 [ 4 ] , the tax on Social Security depends on provisional income, which is your other income plus half your benefits. Say the couple files jointly with $40,000 in pension and IRA income, and his $16,800 a year is the household’s only benefit.
 Their provisional income is $48,400, which is above the $44,000 [ 4 ] adjusted base amount for joint returns. Under the statute’s formula, $9,740 of his benefits become taxable, which puts their AGI at $49,740.
 With the checks paused, taxable benefits drop to zero and AGI falls to $40,000. That lets them convert $9,740 from a traditional IRA into a Roth and still land at the AGI they had with the checks on. They can repeat it each year of the pause, moving money into a Roth before required withdrawals begin. The cost is cash flow: the missing $16,800 has to come from savings.
 Medicare Will Bill You Directly While Checks Are Off
 Part B premiums can’t be deducted from suspended benefits. Instead, Medicare sends a bill, and if you don’t pay on time, you can lose Part B coverage [ 3 ] . Set up automatic payment from your bank. The standard 2027 premium is $209.40 [ 5 ] a month, up from $202.90, and was announced November 17, 2026. Joint filers with income above $224,000 [ 5 ] pay $293.10 or more. That surcharge is based on income from two years earlier, so keep conversions below that line. Anyone also receiving SSI loses eligibility once retirement benefits are suspended.
 Three Moves Before You Pause
 Count the household cost. Add any spousal check on your record to your own. Then compare the total against a break-even age in the low 80s.
 Size your conversions. Convert only up to your old AGI, a bracket limit, or the IRMAA threshold , whichever comes first.
 Consider trust fund risk. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that the combined trust funds will be depleted in 2034 [ 6 ] , after which 83% of scheduled benefits would still be paid.
 Suspension, spousal benefits, and conversion sizing all interact, so it’s worth running the numbers with a fiduciary advisor or CPA before you call SSA.
